name: Neck Arthritis (Cervical Spondylosis)
also_called: degenerative disk disease of the neck
seo_title: Neck Arthritis Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: Stiff, achy neck from arthritis? Physical therapy for cervical spondylosis in North Palm Beach, one-on-one since 1991. Medicare accepted. Call 561-624-4263.
lede: Neck arthritis can make turning your head stiff and sore, and physical therapy focuses on restoring motion and strength so daily tasks feel easier.
what_it_is: Cervical spondylosis is the medical term for age-related wear in the neck. Over time, the disks between the seven neck vertebrae dry out and lose height, the small facet joints carry more load, and bone spurs can form along the edges of the bones. Ligaments may stiffen as well. These changes can leave the neck stiff and sore, and in some people they crowd the nerves or the spinal cord.

These changes are extremely common. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons and Mayo Clinic, more than 85% of people over 60 are affected, and Cleveland Clinic notes the changes usually begin in your 30s. Many people with these findings on an X-ray have no symptoms. Repetitive neck work, earlier neck injuries, family history and smoking raise the odds of trouble.
symptoms: A grinding or popping feeling when you turn your head
Muscle spasms or knots in the neck
Tingling, numbness or weakness in the arms if a nerve is pinched
Clumsy hands, poor balance or trouble walking if the spinal cord is affected
causes: Age-related drying and shrinking of the neck disks
Bone spurs along the vertebrae and facet joints
Work or hobbies with repetitive neck motion, awkward positions or overhead work
Obesity and heavy lifting with poor form

how_therapy_helps.intro: Exercise sits at the center of nonsurgical care. Mayo Clinic describes physical therapy that stretches and strengthens the neck and shoulder muscles as possibly one of the best treatments for the pain and stiffness of cervical spondylosis, and notes that traction helps some people when nerve roots are being pinched. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons lists physical therapy as a first-line treatment. The 2017 JOSPT neck pain guideline supports pairing manual therapy with mixed exercise for long-lasting neck pain with stiffness.
methods: Joint mobilization and guided range-of-motion exercises target stiff segments so turning to check traffic or looking up becomes easier.
Exercises for the neck, shoulder blade and upper back muscles help them hold your head up comfortably through the day.
Regular stretching of tight neck and shoulder muscles eases stiffness without forcing painful end ranges.
Traction when a nerve is involved
If arm symptoms suggest a pinched nerve root, gentle traction may help create space, as Mayo Clinic notes some people benefit from it.
Your therapist reviews screen height, reading posture and sleep setup, and helps you stay active, which Mayo Clinic says helps speed recovery.

first_visit: Your evaluation measures how far your neck turns, tilts and bends, and which motions bring on pain. Your therapist checks strength, sensation and reflexes in your arms and screens balance, walking and hand coordination for signs of spinal cord involvement. Posture, upper back mobility and your daily demands, such as driving or desk work, round out the picture and shape the plan you start that day.
recovery: The wear itself does not reverse. Cleveland Clinic notes that it generally progresses with time, although symptoms do not necessarily get worse along with it. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says that in most cases cervical spondylosis responds well to conservative treatment, and describes a typical course of physical therapy as 6 to 8 weeks with 2 to 3 sessions a week. Many people then keep up a home routine to protect the motion and strength they regain. Arm or spinal cord symptoms follow a different course and need physician follow-up.
self_care: Keep moving. Mayo Clinic notes that staying active helps recovery, even if you need to modify some exercises for a while.
Use heat or ice to ease sore neck muscles, with a cloth layer to protect your skin.
If you use a soft neck brace, wear it only for short periods, since longer use can weaken neck muscles and add stiffness.
Raise screens and reading material closer to eye level and take regular breaks from looking down.
Lift with good form and avoid heavy loads that strain your neck.
see_a_doctor: Sudden numbness or weakness in your arms or legs needs prompt medical attention.
Loss of bladder or bowel control needs emergency care.
Trouble walking, loss of balance or weakness in the hands or legs can signal spinal cord compression and should be seen by a physician quickly.
New clumsiness or coordination problems in your hands warrant a physician visit.
Severe neck pain after a fall or car accident needs emergency evaluation.
Go to the emergency room for intense neck pain accompanied by a high fever.

faqs.q: Can you reverse arthritis in the neck?
faqs.a: The disk and bone changes of cervical spondylosis do not go away, but how you feel is a separate question. Cleveland Clinic notes that while the wear tends to progress, symptoms do not necessarily worsen with it. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons points out that nearly half of middle-aged and older adults have worn disks that cause no pain. Treatment aims at pain, stiffness and function.

faqs.q: What exercises are good for neck arthritis?
faqs.a: Mayo Clinic recommends exercises that stretch and strengthen the neck and shoulder muscles, taught by a physical therapist. Programs usually combine gentle range-of-motion work, strengthening for the upper back and shoulder blade muscles, and posture practice. The right mix depends on which motions are stiff or painful and whether a nerve is involved, so it is worth having a therapist set the starting point.

faqs.q: Is heat or ice better for arthritis in the neck?
faqs.a: Either can help. Mayo Clinic says applying heat or ice to the neck can ease sore neck muscles, and neither is clearly better for everyone with cervical spondylosis. Many people simply use whichever feels better at the time. Keep a cloth layer between the pack and your skin, limit each session, and stop if your skin becomes very red, numb or irritated.

Yes. Both the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons and Cleveland Clinic list headaches among the symptoms of cervical spondylosis, along with neck pain and stiffness. A headache that is sudden and severe, or comes with fever, weakness or confusion, is a different matter and needs urgent medical care instead of a therapy appointment.

faqs.q: Can arthritis in the neck cause arm numbness?
faqs.a: It can. Bone spurs and disk changes may narrow the openings where nerve roots leave the spine, causing tingling, numbness or weakness in the arm. If the central spinal canal narrows, the spinal cord itself can be squeezed. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons lists trouble walking, loss of balance and hand or leg weakness as warning signs that need a physician's evaluation.

faqs.q: Is neck arthritis the same as degenerative disc disease?
faqs.a: The terms overlap. Mayo Clinic describes cervical spondylosis as a general term for age-related wear and tear affecting the spinal disks in your neck. It includes disks drying out and shrinking, bone spurs, herniated disks and stiffening ligaments. Degenerative disk disease usually refers to the disk part of that picture, while spondylosis covers the whole set of changes.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M47.812 (Spondylosis without myelopathy or radiculopathy, cervical region) verified on icd10data.com. Cases with radiculopathy or myelopathy use other M47 codes.
The 6 to 8 weeks, 2 to 3 sessions per week figure comes from the OrthoInfo page; confirm it matches typical clinic plans of care.
The JOSPT 2017 guideline's chronic mobility-deficit recommendations include dry needling, laser and mechanical traction; these were left out because they are outside the clinic's listed services.
The headache FAQ includes a general caution about sudden severe headache with fever or weakness; that caution is general safety guidance, not from a specific cited page.
The heat/ice FAQ intentionally gives no session time because the cited Mayo spondylosis page does not specify one.
